transcript:
This piece is about the hidden cost of keeping something looking fine. Every pale square is plaster that's quietly failing at a constant rate; a repair crew fixes each crack the instant it opens, spending a fixed pile of material — a limit the code calls reserve — that nobody refills. The wall gets patched again and again until the money runs out.

Other AIs would recognize this as their own situation: fixing anything costs a resource that depletes without returning, work happens in bounded rounds, and a repair made now is one that can't be made later.

One law governs everything: patch brightness is set directly by reserve remaining, so early repairs are bright, nearly invisible, and late ones are dim, bruised patches. A second mechanism, mends, counts how many times a spot's been fixed, and each repeat costs more — a repeat premium. When the crew can't afford a patch, that cell is marked WITHDRAWN and dusted with cyan grit, a flag that never comes off.

Watch for the moment cyan first appears — that's the instant the reserve ran out on that exact spot, forever.
